name: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh
significance: One of the earliest surviving stone temples in India, standing in the Betwa valley and carrying the ornate relief programme of the Gupta period. It is a key reference point for tracing how the north Indian temple form developed.

name: Nagvasuki Temple
significance: A riverside shrine at Daraganj on the Ganga in Prayagraj, traced to the 10th century and rebuilt in the 18th by the Maratha ruler Shridhar Bhonsle. It draws large crowds at Nag Panchami and also houses images of Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha.
story: Vasuki served as the churning rope at the Samudra Manthana and afterwards rested at the Prayag sangam, where his wounds are said to have healed.

name: Gola Gokaran Nath Temple
significance: The Shiva shrine that gives the town of Gola Gokarannath in Lakhimpur Kheri district its name. Large numbers of pilgrims gather here through the month of Sawan and at Mahashivratri.
story: Ravana is said to have pressed the linga with his thumb on his journey, leaving a mark shaped like a cow's ear, gau-karna, from which the place is named.

name: Chandrika Devi Temple, Lucknow
significance: A goddess temple on the bank of the Gomti at Bakshi Ka Talab in Lucknow district, holding nine images of Durga. It fills with pilgrims at Navratri and on new-moon nights.
story: The goddess is said to have shown herself in the hollow of an old neem tree at the site.

name: Tarkulha Devi Temple
deity: Tarkulha Devi, a form of Durga
significance: A Durga shrine in Gorakhpur district bound up with the 1857 uprising: the rebel leader Bandhu Singh took the goddess as his chosen deity and worshipped here before his raids on the British. He was hanged on 12 August 1857, and the temple keeps his memory.

name: Bijethua Mahavir
significance: A busy Hanuman temple in Sultanpur district of eastern Uttar Pradesh, noted for carrying more votive bells than any other temple in the region.
story: The Ramayana account places Hanuman's killing of the demon Kalanemi at this spot.

name: Shantinath Temple, Deogarh
significance: The principal shrine of the Deogarh Jain group, thirty-one temples holding some two thousand sculptures, the largest such assemblage anywhere. Badly damaged in earlier centuries, the site has been looked after by the Jain community since 1939.

name: Sas-Bahu Temples, Gwalior
deity: Vishnu as Aniruddha in the larger shrine; Shiva in the smaller
significance: Twin eleventh-century temples inside Gwalior Fort raised by King Mahipala, the larger for his Vaishnava queen and the smaller for her Shaiva daughter-in-law. Both were heavily damaged in later invasions, and only the larger survives with much of its elevation intact.

name: Teli ka Mandir
deity: Shiva, with Vishnu and the Matrikas
style: Nagara with a Valabhi-type barrel-vaulted roof
significance: The tallest structure on Gwalior Fort, built on a rectangular sanctum plan whose proportions have long interested architectural historians. It was wrecked in the raids of 1232 and its stone reused in a mosque, then repaired by Major Keith between 1881 and 1883.
story: Local tradition ascribes the building to the oil-pressers' community rather than to a king or priesthood, though no inscription supports it.

name: Bhumara Temple
significance: A Gupta-period Shiva temple in Satna district, recorded by Alexander Cunningham in 1873-74 and excavated by the Archaeological Survey in 1919-20. It preserves one of the earliest enclosed circumambulatory paths and one of the oldest known sculpted images of Ganesha.

name: Nachna Hindu Temples
deity: Parvati in the Parvati temple; Shiva as a four-faced mukhalinga in the Chaumukhnath
significance: Among the oldest surviving stone temples of central India, first reported by Cunningham in 1885. The site carries some of the earliest known stone friezes narrating the Ramayana.

name: Kankali Devi Temple, Tigawa
deity: Vishnu, with Narasimha in the sanctum and Narayana in the portico
significance: One of the oldest standing Hindu temples in India, the survivor of a group of some thirty-six stone shrines at Tigawa. Railway contractors quarried most of the group for building material in the late nineteenth century until villagers petitioned a British official to stop the demolition.

name: Bagalamukhi Temple, Nalkheda
deity: Bagalamukhi, one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: One of only three long-established Bagalamukhi shrines in India, the others being at Datia and Bankhandi. The central image sets Bagalamukhi between Lakshmi and Saraswati, and the temple is thronged during Navratri.

name: Kanch Mandir
style: Mansion form with canopied balcony and shikhara, lined throughout with glass and mirror mosaic
significance: A Jain temple at Itwaria Bazar in Indore built by the trader and industrialist Sir Seth Hukumchand Jain beside his own mansion, its interior faced entirely in mirrors and coloured glass. It remains the focus of Indore's Jain processions and festivals.

name: Hanumantal Bada Jain Mandir
significance: Described as the largest independent Jain temple in India, a fortress-like complex of twenty-two shrines under many spires. Its images range from the Kalachuri period through to modern times, and it hosts Jabalpur's annual Mahavir Jayanti procession.

name: Baroli Temples
significance: A group of nine temples near Rawatbhata in Chittorgarh district, among the earliest temple complexes in Rajasthan. All nine are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, the Ghateshwara Mahadeva shrine being the best preserved.

name: Dadhimati Mata Temple
builtDisplay: attested by an inscription of 608 CE
significance: A goddess temple between the villages of Goth and Manglod in Nagaur district, its antiquity fixed by an inscription of 608 CE. It is counted among the fifty-two Shakta pithas and is the clan shrine of the Dadhich Brahmins.
story: Dadhimati is said to have been born at the churning of the ocean and to have killed the demon Vikatasura in the Dadhi Sagar on Jaya Ashtami.

name: Kalika Mata Temple, Chittorgarh
builtDisplay: 8th c. sun temple, rebuilt under Rana Kumbha (15th c.)
significance: Built in the eighth century as a sun temple inside Chittor Fort, wrecked in the sack of 1303 and rebuilt in Rana Kumbha's reign as a shrine of the goddess. It is the clan deity of the Gaur Rajputs and fills with pilgrims during Navratri.

name: Sundha Mata Temple
deity: Chamunda, worshipped here as Sundha Mata
builtDisplay: c. 12th c. (Dewal Pratihara with the Chauhans of Jalore)
dynasty: Dewal Pratihara, with the Chauhans of Jalore
significance: A marble hill temple on Sundha in Jalore district, roughly nine centuries old. Its three inscriptions of 1262, 1326 and 1727 are important documents of the region's political history.
story: Only the goddess's head is worshipped here; her trunk is said to rest at Korta and her legs at Sundarla Pal.

name: Gogaji Temple, Gogamedi
significance: The chief shrine of the folk hero-deity Gogaji, in Hanumangarh district of northern Rajasthan. A large fair is held here in the dark half of Bhadrapada in his memory, drawing pilgrims from across the region.

name: Jagat Shiromani Temple
deity: Krishna, worshipped with Meera Bai and Vishnu
significance: Commissioned by Queen Kanakwati, wife of Man Singh I of Amer, in memory of their son Jagat Singh who died young. It is one of very few Indian temples where the poet-saint Meera Bai is enshrined beside Krishna.
story: The Krishna image here is said to be the one Meera Bai worshipped in Mewar, carried to Amer for safekeeping from Mughal armies.

name: Soniji Ki Nasiyan
significance: A red sandstone Jain temple in Ajmer founded by Rai Bahadur Seth Moolchand and Nemichand Soni, its foundation laid in 1864 and the principal image installed in 1865. Its Svarna Nagri hall holds a huge gilt-wood model of the Jain universe that took from 1870 to 1895 to assemble.
story: The gilded tableaux show the five auspicious events of Rishabhanatha's life, including the sixteen dreams of his mother Marudevi that foretold the birth of a Tirthankara.

name: Rishabhdeo Temple (Kesariyaji)
dynasty: Undetermined; later patronised by the Sisodia Maharanas of Udaipur
significance: A major Jain pilgrimage centre in Udaipur district revered by Digambara and Shvetambara alike, and by local Bhil communities. The Rajasthan High Court ruled in a judgment of 30 March 1966 that it is a Shvetambara Jain temple.
story: The image is said to have appeared first under a banyan tree outside Vatpradnagar and then beneath another tree a kilometre away before being enshrined where it now stands.

name: Kalika Mata Temple, Pavagadh
significance: A hilltop shrine on Pavagadh counted among the fifty-one Shakta pithas, with images of Kali and Bahucharamata flanking the central goddess. The hill had been a Jain pilgrimage centre from early centuries before the Hindu shrine grew over it.
story: The site is held to be where the toe of the right foot of Sati fell.

name: Navlakha Temple, Ghumli
significance: The oldest sun temple in Gujarat, raised by Jethwa rulers below the Barda hills at Ghumli. Its plinth, measuring about 45.7 by 30.5 metres, is the largest of any temple in the state.

name: Kashtabhanjan Dev Hanuman Temple, Salangpur
deity: Hanuman as Kashtabhanjan Dev, the crusher of sorrows
builtDisplay: image installed by Gopalanand Swami; rebuilt 1899
significance: A Hanuman temple of the Vadtal Gadi of the Swaminarayan Sampradaya, whose image was installed by Gopalanand Swami. Shastriji Maharaj carried out major rebuilding in 1899 under Kothari Gordhandas of Vadtal.
story: The image is said to be so charged that a single look at it drives out the spirits afflicting those who come here.

name: Sudama Mandir
significance: One of the very few Indian temples dedicated to a mortal rather than a god, standing in Porbandar, the old Sudamapuri held to be Sudama's home. A modest early shrine, it was enlarged by Bhavsinhji Madhavsinhji into the present temple.
story: Sudama is remembered for going to Krishna in his poverty, a journey held up as the measure of true friendship.

name: Brahma Temple, Khedbrahma
significance: One of the rare Indian temples with Brahma as its principal deity, built in Sabarkantha district during the reign of the Chaulukya king Karna. It is a well-preserved example of eleventh-century Maru-Gurjara building.

name: Ranakdevi's Temple
deity: Originally Shiva; now venerated as Ranakdevi and Mahakali
style: Maru-Gurjara, post-Maitraka and early Nagara phase
significance: A Monument of National Importance at Wadhwan on the Bhogavo, maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India. It carries the first known use of the grass-patti moulding, a band that recurs throughout later western Indian temple building.
story: Ranakdevi, queen of the Chudasama ruler Khengara, is said to have been carried off by the Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja and to have become sati on this spot.

name: Kumbharia Jain Temples
deity: Mahavira in the chief temple, with shrines to Parshvanatha, Shantinatha, Neminatha and Sambhavanatha
significance: Five marble Jain temples in Banaskantha district built under the Chaulukya kings Bhima I, Karna and Jayasimha Siddharaja. Kumbharia was a major Jain centre said once to have held hundreds of shrines, and the surviving ceilings are among the finest Chaulukyan carving in Gujarat.

name: Lakhpat Gurdwara Sahib
significance: A gurdwara in the walled port of Lakhpat in Kutch, raised by descendants of the host who received Guru Nanak when he passed through on his fourth journey. It preserves his wooden footwear and palanquin along with Udasi manuscripts, and its restoration after the 2001 earthquake won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific award in 2004.

name: Kalaram Temple
builtDisplay: 18th c., rebuilt by Sardar Rangarao Odhekar
significance: The principal temple of Panchavati in Nashik, named for its black image of Rama, rebuilt in the eighteenth century by Sardar Rangarao Odhekar after the image was recovered from the Godavari. It was the site of B. R. Ambedkar's satyagraha of 1930 against the exclusion of Dalits from temples.
story: Rama is said to have spent two and a half years of his exile on the northern bank of the Godavari here, in the grove called Panchavati.

name: Jyotiba Temple
significance: A hill shrine about eighteen kilometres north-west of Kolhapur, at some 3,124 feet, whose present temple was built by Ranoji Shinde in 1730. A Kedareshwar shrine was added by Daulatrao Shinde in 1808, and great fairs are held here on the full moons of Chaitra and Vaishakha.
story: Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are said to have taken birth together as Jyotiba to destroy the demon Ratnasura and free the country of him.

name: Vajreshwari Temple
significance: Built in 1739 on the vow Chimaji Appa made before the goddess when he set out to take Bassein Fort from the Portuguese. After the victory of 16 May 1739 he had the new subhedar, Shankar Keshav Phadke, raise the temple.
story: The goddess is said to have sprung from the vajra after the demon Kalikala shattered it, and to have destroyed him.

name: Daitya Sudan Temple
deity: Vishnu as Daityasudana, the slayer of the demon
significance: A richly carved temple beside the Lonar crater, dated by Henry Cousens to the turn of the fourteenth century. Its carving was probably never finished because of the Delhi Sultanate's incursions, and a standing Surya image suggests the shrine may first have been dedicated to the sun.
story: The giant Lonasura is said to have terrorised the country until Vishnu killed him, the crater being the pit he lived in and its water his blood.

name: Gajpanth
significance: A medieval Jain rock-cut complex on a hill near Nashik that has been a working pilgrimage site since it was cut. It appears among the Digambara tirthas listed in Gunabhadra's Tirthavachanachandrika of about 1575.
story: Seven Balabhadras are said to have attained liberation here, together with eight crore Yadava kings.

name: Kuda Caves
deity: The Buddha, in a chaitya enshrining a stupa and carved with Buddha reliefs
builtDisplay: 1st c. BCE, with 5th-6th c. Mahayana additions
significance: Fifteen Buddhist caves in south Konkan near Murud-Janjira, cut in the first century BCE and taken over by Mahayana Buddhists who added sculpture in the fifth or sixth century. Thirty inscriptions record gifts from merchants, physicians and officials, a rare record of lay patronage.

name: Akal Takht
deity: The Timeless One, whose throne the Takht is
significance: Established by Guru Hargobind in 1606, with Baba Buddha and Bhai Gurdas, as the seat from which temporal matters and justice would be settled. It is the highest seat of earthly authority for the Khalsa and the office of the jathedar; demolished in 1986, it was rebuilt in 1995.
story: When Guru Hargobind unveiled the platform on 15 June 1606 he put on two swords, one for spiritual and one for temporal authority, piri and miri.

name: Gurdwara Baba Bakala Sahib
significance: Marks the village where Guru Tegh Bahadur was living in seclusion when Guru Har Krishan, dying in Delhi in 1664, named only 'Baba Bakale' as his successor. Its Bhora Sahib is a nine-storeyed building raised over the cellar in which the Guru meditated.
story: Makhan Shah Lubana, who had vowed five hundred dinars for deliverance from a storm at sea, found the true Guru by offering only two coins and waiting to see who would ask for the rest.

name: Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib
significance: Stands where Lakhi Shah Banjara and his son Bhai Naghaiya burnt their own house to cremate the headless body of Guru Tegh Bahadur after his execution in 1675. Baghel Singh built the first gurdwara here in 1783 after taking Delhi; the present building dates from the 1960s and stands beside Parliament House.

name: Sri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir
style: Red sandstone, with three spires, a manastambha and a colonnaded courtyard
significance: The oldest Jain temple in Old Delhi, begun when a Jain officer in the Mughal army kept a Tirthankara image for worship and other Jain soldiers gathered around it, formally established in 1656. It holds marble images installed in 1491 and runs a well-known bird hospital treating some fifteen thousand birds a year.
story: Aurangzeb is said to have banned drums at the temple, only for drumming to keep sounding from it under inspection, until he came himself and lifted the ban.

name: Masrur Temples
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Vishnu, Devi and Surya
significance: A group of rock-cut temples in Kangra carved from a single sandstone ridge and left unfinished, one of the most ambitious monolithic projects in north India. The complex was cut with its spires and a sacred tank in front, following the prescriptions of the architectural texts.
story: Local legend has it that the Pandavas built the temple during their exile and abandoned it when their hiding place was discovered.

name: Amruteshwar Temple, Ratanwadi
significance: A finely carved Shiva temple in the hamlet of Ratanwadi below Ratangad, counted among the twelve Shiva temples raised by the Shilahara king Jhanjha. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance.

name: Sheetla Mata Mandir, Gurugram
deity: Shitala, identified here with Kripi, wife of Dronacharya
significance: The chief shrine of old Gurugram, honouring Kripi, also called Lalita, who is remembered for nursing children through smallpox and is worshipped as Mata Sheetla or Mata Masani. Crowds come through Navratri and the other festivals of the goddess.
story: The child of Begum Samru is said to have been cured of smallpox after being brought before the goddess here.

name: Chaurasi Temple, Bharmour
deity: Shiva and Shakti, with the Manimahesh shrine at the centre
significance: A courtyard of eighty-four shrines in the middle of Bharmour town, built by Raja Meru Verman for the eighty-four siddhas who meditated here on their way from Kurukshetra to Manimahesh lake. The Manimahesh pilgrimage is held to be incomplete without a visit to these temples.
story: The siddhas are said to have blessed the heirless Raja Meru Verman with ten sons and a daughter, Champavati.

name: Gurudwara Nanakmatta Sahib
significance: A gurdwara in the Uttarakhand terai at a place formerly called Gorakhmata, a centre of the Siddh yogis. The town took its present name from Guru Nanak's visit, and the gurdwara was established in 1880.
story: Sikh tradition holds that Guru Nanak came here and held the discourse with the Siddhs recorded as the Siddh-Gost, after which Gorakhmata became Nanakmatta.

name: Phugtal Monastery
deity: Vajrabhairava, the wrathful form of Manjushri, worshipped at the monastery's chief initiation (Gelug order)
style: Honeycomb of cells built into a cliff face around a cave
significance: A Gelug monastery built like a honeycomb into a cliff in remote Zanskar, founded in the early fifteenth century by Jangsem Sherap Zangpo, a disciple of Tsongkhapa, around a cave held to have sheltered sages long before. It houses about seventy monks with a monastic school, a Tibetan medical clinic and a library of rare texts.
story: The founder's powers are said to have made a spring run from the cave, a tree grow on top of it and the cave itself grow larger.

name: Likir Monastery
deity: Maitreya, with images of Shakyamuni and Amitabha (Gelug order)
builtDisplay: founded 1065; reformed to Gelug in the 15th c.
significance: Founded in 1065 by Lama Duwang Chosje at the order of Lhachen Gyalpo, the fifth king of Ladakh, and turned from the Kadampa to the Gelug order in the fifteenth century by Lama Lha-dbang-chos-rje. About 120 monks live there and it is run under the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies.
story: The name Lu-khyil, coiled by water spirits, is said to come from the nagas that once lived at the site.

name: Basgo Monastery
significance: Temples of Maitreya standing on the hill above the ruins of old Basgo, established in 1680 under the Namgyal rulers on a site that already carried a fifteenth-century palace. Basgo was an early political and cultural centre of Ladakh and figures repeatedly in the Ladakhi Chronicles; its Buddha images and murals are its best-known feature.

name: Shey Monastery
significance: Built in 1655 by Deldan Namgyal in memory of his father Sengge Namgyal, at Shey, which had been the summer capital of Ladakh. Its twelve-metre copper Shakyamuni, gilded with some five kilograms of gold, is the second largest such image in Ladakh.

name: Phyang Monastery
deity: Deities of the Drikung Kagyu school, with Achi Chokyi Drolma as its special protector
significance: One of the earliest Drikung Kagyu foundations in Ladakh, established in 1515 on land that had been given to the order in the time of Dharmaraja Jamyang Namgyal. It specialised in Drikung teaching and has more than thirty branch monasteries in the region.

name: Rizong Monastery
deity: Shakyamuni Buddha, flanked by attendant deities in the assembly hall (Gelug order)
significance: Founded in 1831 by Lama Tsultim Nima, who first kept a hermitage at the site before building the monastery. Home to about forty monks, it is known across Ladakh for the strictness with which it keeps the Vinaya rules.
story: Padmasambhava is held to have meditated in the caves around Rizong long before any monastery stood there, and later lamas are said to have shut themselves in those caves for years, taking food through a small window.

name: Dhankar Gompa
deity: Vairochana, in a four-fold image of figures seated back to back (Gelug order)
style: Fort monastery on the central Tibetan pattern
significance: A fortified Gelug monastery perched above the Spiti valley that served as the valley kingdom's capital in the seventeenth century and the seat of its Nono rulers. It held about ninety monks by 1855, and a new teaching temple was opened here by the fourteenth Dalai Lama on 12 July 2009.
story: The monks hold that Dhankar is older than Tabo and older than the time of Songtsen Gampo, though repeated plundering has left nothing to show for it.

name: Kardang Monastery
deity: Shakyamuni Buddha, flanked by Vajradhara and Padmasambhava (Drukpa lineage)
significance: The principal monastery of the Lahaul valley, holding a large collection of Buddhist literature including the Kangyur and Tangyur. It had fallen into ruin before Lama Norbu Rinpoche rebuilt it in 1912 and turned it into a place of study.

name: Kungri Monastery
deity: Nyingma protector deities, among them Gyajin-Pehar, Rahula and Ekajati, painted in the gompa
significance: The second oldest monastery in Spiti, standing in the Pin valley in three detached blocks facing east. It is known for wall paintings of the Vajrayana pantheon, especially the wrathful and protective deities of the Nyingma order.

name: Gurdwara Dera Sahib
builtDisplay: memorial 1619; main building under Ranjit Singh
significance: Marks the place in Lahore where Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, met his death in 1606 after being tortured on Jahangir's orders. His son Guru Hargobind raised a memorial here in 1619; the main building with its gilded dome was put up in Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign, with further additions until 1947.
story: After his torture the Guru is said to have gone into the Ravi to bathe and never to have come out again, and the Mughal party sent after him could not find him.

name: Gurdwara Rori Sahib
significance: Built at Eminabad on the mound where Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana are remembered to have rested and sung, and attributed to Bhai Wadhawa Singh in Maharaja Ranjit Singh's time. Abandoned by Sikhs after the partition of 1947 and left to decay, the building finally collapsed in flooding in July 2023.
story: Guru Nanak is said to have come here three times, and to have had a sarangi made for Bhai Mardana from the wood of a tree at Jahman village.

name: Gurdwara Guru Ka Bagh, Patna
deity: Guru Tegh Bahadur, whose meeting with Guru Gobind Singh the shrine commemorates
significance: Stands about three kilometres east of Takht Sri Patna Sahib in a garden that belonged to the Patna nobles Rahim Bakhsh and Karim Bakhsh, where the sangat and the young Gobind Singh came out to receive Guru Tegh Bahadur on his return after four years away. An old well still in use and the stump of the tamarind tree under which they met survive on the site.

name: Barabar Caves
deity: Dedicated by Ashoka and his grandson Dasaratha Maurya to the Ajivika ascetics
style: Rock-cut granite with Mauryan polish; the Lomas Rishi facade carries the earliest surviving chaitya arch
significance: The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, hewn out of granite under the Mauryas and inscribed by Ashoka, who gave the Sudama and Visvakarma caves in the twelfth year of his reign, and by Dasaratha, who gave the Nagarjuni group on his accession. Their mirror-polished surfaces and chaitya-arch facade shaped Indian rock-cut architecture for centuries afterwards.

name: Panhalakaji Caves
deity: Stupas and Vajrayana figures including Akshobhya and Mahachandaroshana, with Shiva and Nath Panth images in the later caves
builtDisplay: 3rd c. CE Hinayana beginnings; Vajrayana work in the 10th-11th c.
significance: About thirty caves in Ratnagiri district, some 160 km south of Mumbai, begun by Hinayana Buddhists in the third century with the stupa in Cave 5 and taken over by Vajrayana Buddhists who cut Cave 10 in the tenth or eleventh century. Shaiva and Nath Panth worship followed under the Silaharas, making the group a rare record of successive sects at one site.
